text: Adapting large language models (LLMs) to downstream tasks is frequently constrained by GPU memory.
During full fine-tuning with Adam, memory is dominated by optimizer states, gradients, and activations, far exceeding static weight storage.
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) and low-memory algorithms exploit structural redundancies to alleviate these bottlenecks.
This note examines architectural decomposition, quantization, and gradient projection paradigms, evaluates memory-throughput trade-offs, and outlines a controlled single-GPU experiment.
Restricting updates to low-rank or sparse subspaces while freezing base weights eliminates optimizer states and gradient buffers for frozen parameters.
Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) assumes weight updates during adaptation possess a low intrinsic rank.
Rather than updating full matrices directly, LoRA freezes the pre-trained model weights and injects trainable rank decomposition matrices into each layer of the Transformer architecture.
For weight dimensions d × k, updates factor into two low-rank matrices of rank r (d, k).
Compared to GPT-3 175B fine-tuned with Adam, LoRA can reduce the number of trainable parameters by 10,000 times and the GPU memory requirement by 3 times.

Crucially, this measured saving was recorded specifically on GPT-3 175B using 16-bit Adam; it cannot be transferred naively to smaller models where intermediate activation tensors dominate total VRAM.
Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation (DoRA) investigates the learning dynamics gap between full fine-tuning and LoRA.
Full fine-tuning exhibits negative correlations between magnitude and directional updates, whereas LoRA exhibits a positive correlation.
To bridge this gap, DoRA decomposes the pre-trained weight into its magnitude and directional components and finetunes both of them, decomposing the directional component with LoRA.
Low-rank directional updates maintain parameter efficiency while magnitude vectors scale column norms independently.
Furthermore, DoRA can be merged with the pre-trained weight before inference, thereby not introducing any additional latency.
However, column norm tracking induces slight runtime and activation overhead compared to standard LoRA.
Ben-Zaken et al. demonstrated that BitFit is a sparse fine-tuning method where only the bias terms of the model are modified.
In BERTBASE and BERTLARGE, bias parameters make up 0.09% and 0.08% of the total number of parameters in each model, respectively.
Modifying under 0.1% of parameters minimizes optimizer overhead.
However, modern generative architectures routinely omit bias terms in linear layers.
Consequently, BitFit cannot be transferred directly to modern autoregressive backbones without structural modifications.

To evaluate these methods under controlled consumer limits, we specify an experiment on a single 24GB GPU (RTX 4090, locked clocks).
The backbone is Mistral-7B-v0.1, adapted on Alpaca and evaluated on GSM8K and CommonsenseQA.
Configurations share a harness: PyTorch 2.x, Flash\-Attention-2, bfloat16 precision, sequence length 2,048 tokens, and effective batch size 16 (micro-batch 1, 16 accumulation steps).
Full activation checkpointing is enabled across all decoder layers to recompute activations during backward passes, isolating parameter and optimizer footprints.
Optimizers are fixed: AdamW with 32-bit master states for LoRA, DoRA, and AdaLoRA; 8-bit blockwise AdamW for GaLore; and Paged 32-bit AdamW for QLoRA (1=0.9, 2=0.999, weight decay 0.01).

We compare four setups: (1) LoRA (r=16, =32 on all linear projections); (2) DoRA (matching r=16, =32); (3) QLoRA (4-bit NF4 base, double quantization, r=16); and (4) GaLore (rank 128, subspace updates every 200 steps).

Protocol: (i) Post-warmup peak VRAM, tracking torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() and torch.cuda.max_memory_reserved() between steps 50 and 250 across identical 2,048-token inputs; (ii) Steady-state throughput (tokens per second, excluding evaluation and checkpoint I/O); and (iii) Accuracy on held-out benchmarks.
This ensures memory comparisons reflect empirical measurement rather than inferred parameter counts.
Several boundaries restrict the transfer of published findings.
Reported memory reductions measured on very large models do not transfer proportionally to smaller architectures where activation memory dominates over parameter and optimizer states.
Architectural differences such as the complete omission of bias terms in modern transformer families prevent direct application of bias-only tuning without structural modifications.
Furthermore, memory savings achieved through weight quantization incur runtime latency penalties depending on hardware bandwidth and kernel implementation.
